latest_release.body:
## What's Changed
* chore(bun): track offsets for bun-v1.4.3 by @dhiaayachi in https://github.com/spinningfactory/kloak/pull/323
* chore(deps): bump golang.org/x/sys from 0.48.0 to 0.49.0 by @dependabot[bot] in https://github.com/spinningfactory/kloak/pull/324
* chore(deps): bump golang.org/x/net from 0.59.0 to 0.61.0 by @dependabot[bot] in https://github.com/spinningfactory/kloak/pull/325
* feat(ebpf): only rewrite host-scoped secrets on connections whose SNI is the host by @dhiaayachi in https://github.com/spinningfactory/kloak/pull/329
* ci(coverage): fix unit + e2e merge that under-reported coverage (55% → ~77%) by @dhiaayachi in https://github.com/spinningfactory/kloak/pull/330
* perf(ebpf): shrink the TLS data-plane programs without behaviour changes by @dhiaayachi in https://github.com/spinningfactory/kloak/pull/332
* feat(ebpf): allocate pinned virtual IPs for watched hosts (--host-resolution=virtual-ip) by @dhiaayachi in https://github.com/spinningfactory/kloak/pull/331
* ci(coverage): merge the coverage of every e2e leg, not just the default one by @dhiaayachi in https://github.com/spinningfactory/kloak/pull/334
* feat(ebpf): rewrite DNS answers to virtual IPs and redirect connects to the real ones (--host-resolution=virtual-ip) by @dhiaayachi in https://github.com/spinningfactory/kloak/pull/333
* chore(bun): track offsets for bun-v1.4.4 by @dhiaayachi in https://github.com/spinningfactory/kloak/pull/336
* chore(boringssl): track offsets for 0.20261020.0 by @dhiaayachi in https://github.com/spinningfactory/kloak/pull/337
* feat(ebpf): rewrite DNS only for pods with a secret for the host, attached before the pod's containers start (--host-resolution=virtual-ip) by @dhiaayachi in https://github.com/spinningfactory/kloak/pull/335
* feat(ebpf): take a host-restricted secret's host from the socket (--host-resolution=virtual-ip) by @dhiaayachi in https://github.com/spinningfactory/kloak/pull/338
* feat(ebpf): IPv6 in virtual-ip mode: AAAA answers, connect6 and IPv6 TLS patching (--host-resolution=virtual-ip) by @dhiaayachi in https://github.com/spinningfactory/kloak/pull/339
* feat(controller): attach the DNS rewrite through NRI while the runtime creates the pod sandbox (--host-resolution=virtual-ip) by @dhiaayachi in https://github.com/spinningfactory/kloak/pull/340
* test(e2e): retry the virtual-ip probes' rewritten cases until their secret is synced by @dhiaayachi in https://github.com/spinningfactory/kloak/pull/342
* test(ci): run the privileged BPF tests and an e2e leg on Cilium, and fix what Cilium exposed by @dhiaayachi in https://github.com/spinningfactory/kloak/pull/341
* feat: make virtual-ip the default host resolution, deprecate dns-snoop (#327) by @dhiaayachi in https://github.com/spinningfactory/kloak/pull/344
* ci(nightly): find OpenSSL's x86 GCM code by what it defines, and run discovery on pre-releases by @dhiaayachi in https://github.com/spinningfactory/kloak/pull/345
* feat: remove DNS snooping; virtual IPs are the only host resolution (#327) by @dhiaayachi in https://github.com/spinningfactory/kloak/pull/346
* test(e2e): give the raw TLS demo's requests a timeout by @dhiaayachi in https://github.com/spinningfactory/kloak/pull/347
* fix(ebpf): revoke what a rebound pod lost at once, not at the next sync by @dhiaayachi in https://github.com/spinningfactory/kloak/pull/349
* feat(controller): sync secrets into the BPF maps on Secret events, not every 5 s by @dhiaayachi in https://github.com/spinningfactory/kloak/pull/350
* refactor(ebpf): block in the ring buffer readers instead of polling every second by @dhiaayachi in https://github.com/spinningfactory/kloak/pull/351
* chore(openssl): add offset support for OpenSSL 4.1.0 by @dhiaayachi in https://github.com/spinningfactory/kloak/pull/348
* test(e2e): drop the demos' startup sleeps and the sleeps after deleting a demo by @dhiaayachi in https://github.com/spinningfactory/kloak/pull/352
* test(e2e): give the BoringSSL demo's connec

detail.readme:
Kloak

Secure Your Secrets, Agentless
Kubernetes eBPF HTTPS interceptor. Transparent secret injection without application changes or sidecars.

[![CI](https://github.com/spinningfactory/kloak/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/spinningfactory/kloak/actions/workflows/ci.yml) [![Coverage](https://img.shields.io/endpoint?url=https://gist.githubusercontent.com/dhiaayachi/2d4be46e60ee478d5703d8b009dbd6e9/raw/kloak-coverage.json)](https://gist.github.com/dhiaayachi/2d4be46e60ee478d5703d8b009dbd6e9) [![Go Version](https://img.shields.io/badge/Go-1.26+-00ADD8?logo=go)](https://go.dev/) [![Kubernetes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Kubernetes-1.28+-326CE5?logo=kubernetes)](https://kubernetes.io/) [![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-AGPL--3.0-blue.svg)](LICENSE)
--- Kloak transparently intercepts outbound TLS traffic in Kubernetes using eBPF uprobes, replacing placeholders with real secrets in-kernel by patching the encrypted TLS record on its way out of the pod. Applications never handle actual credentials, and no sidecars or code changes are required. ## Features - **No code changes** -- No SDK, no library, no application modifications. Mount a secret, make HTTPS requests, and Kloak handles the rest. - **Secret isolation** -- Applications only see random shadow values (`kl::…`, same length as the real value). The real value is never written into the pod's memory; it is XOR-patched into the AES-GCM ciphertext in-kernel. - **Zero overhead** -- eBPF uprobes operate in kernel space with negligible latency impact. No userspace proxy or sidecar in the data path. - **Kubernetes native** -- Works with standard Kubernetes Secrets. Enable with a single label. - **Per-pod secret binding** -- A pod can only use the secrets it references in its spec (Secret volume, `secretKeyRef`, `envFrom`). A placeholder sent by any other pod, even one that learned it, goes out unchanged. - **Host and IP filtering** -- Secrets annotated with `getkloak.io/hosts` are only sent to specific destination hostnames or IP addresses, preventing exfiltration to unauthorized servers. Each restricted hostname gets its own virtual IP, so kloak knows which host a connection is for even when hosts share addresses (a CDN, a shared ingress). - **Port-based filtering** -- Secrets annotated with `getkloak.io/port` are restricted to connections on a specific destination port. - **Broad runtime support** -- Hooks into OpenSSL, BoringSSL, and Go's native `crypto/tls`. Works with Python, Node.js, Bun, Go, Rust, Ruby, PHP, curl, and any OpenSSL-linked runtime. ## Quick Start ### Prerequisites - Kubernetes cluster (1.28+) with Linux kernel 5.17+ (6.6+ attaches the tc patch program via TCX; older kernels fall back to a clsact qdisc + cls_bpf filter, see `controller.ebpf.tcAttachMode`) - The virtual IP ranges kloak hands out (default `198.18.0.0/15` and `2001:2::/48`, reserved for benchmarking and never routed) must not be used by the cluster or its nodes. The controller checks this at startup and refuses to start otherwise (`controller.ebpf.virtualIPRange`). - containerd 2.0+ or CRI-O 1.30+ is recommended: through their NRI hook, kloak sets up a pod's DNS rewrite before its containers start, and attaches each container's TLS uprobes before it starts, so even its first request gets the secret. On other runtimes the rewrite is set up as soon as the pod's sandbox runs and a container is attached once the pod's status reports it running, which leaves a short window at pod start (see `controller.nri` in the chart values). - [Helm](https://helm.sh/docs/intro/install/) 3.12+ - `kubectl` configured with cluster access ### Install with Helm ```bash helm repo add kloak https://chart.getkloak.io helm repo update helm install kloak kloak/kloak -n kloak-system --create-namespace kubectl get pods -n kloak-system ``` ### Restarts, upgrades and uninstalling A controller that stops for a restart, a rollout or an upgrade leaves its node's eBPF programs attached (`controller.ebpf.persist`, on by default). They stay pinned under `/sys/fs/bpf/kloak`, the next controller adopts them, and the pods' secrets are rewritten all along. When an upgrade changes the eBPF programs themselves, the new controller loads its own instead, and until it has attached them, the pods' TLS writes carry their placeholders: they fail closed. So do the first upgrade from a version without this, a rollback to one, and turning `controller.ebpf.persist` off: the stopping controller then detaches the programs, as the next one would not adopt them. `helm uninstall` tears the programs down on every node. A pre-delete hook has each controller detach them and remove their pins, then lists the nodes it could not confirm (`uninstall.hook`). A controller also tears them down when it stops and finds its DaemonSet gone, as with `helm uninstall --no-hooks` or a deleted namespace. A node whose controller was not running then, or that left the DaemonSet's scope (its node selector or tolerations changed), keeps them until it reboots. To remove them without a reboot, run `kloak cleanup` as root on the node, for example: ```bash kubectl debug node/ -it --profile=sysadmin --image=ghcr.io/spinningfactory/kloak: \ --custom=<(echo '{"securityContext":{"runAsUser":0}}') -- \ /kloak cleanup --pin-path /host/sys/fs/bpf/kloak --node-lock /host/run/kloak/lock ``` The pinned maps hold the real secrets. As with a running controller's maps, only the node's root can read them. ### Upgrading from v0.2.x and earlier Host-restricted secrets now use virtual IPs (see [Host Verification](#host-verification)) instead of reading the DNS answers pods receive: - Restart kloak-enabled pods after the upgrade. Pods that were already running keep the addresses they resolved, and a connection to a real address gets no host-restricted secret. - If the controller refuses to start because a virtual IP range overlaps an address range of the cluster or a node, set `controller.ebpf.virtualIPRange` to free ranges. ### Labels and Annotations | Key | Type | Scope | Description | |-----|------|-------|-------------| | `getkloak.io/enabled=true` | Label | Secret, Namespace, Pod | Enables Kloak for the target resource. On namespaces and pods, controls webhook scope. On secrets, triggers shadow secret creation. | | `getkloak.io/hosts=host` | Annotation | Secret | Restricts which destination host or IP address a secret can be sent to (single value only) | | `getkloak.io/port=443` | Annotation | Secret | Restricts which destination port a secret can be sent to | | `getkloak.io/managed=true` | Label | Secret | Marks shadow secrets created by Kloak (do not set manually) | ### Try the Demo ```bash # Full demo: creates a Lima VM with K3s, deploys Kloak and sample apps ./examples/setup-demo.sh export KUBECONFIG=/tmp/kloak-k3s.yaml # View logs (should show real secrets in httpbin.org responses) kubectl logs -f -l app=demo-python -n kloak-demo -c demo-app # Cleanup ./examples/destroy-demo.sh ``` ## Architecture Kloak consists of a control plane (controller + webhook) and an eBPF data plane that runs entirely in kernel space. ```mermaid graph TD subgraph Control_Plane [Control Plane] C[Kloak Controller - DaemonSet] W[Mutating Webhook - Deployment] end subgraph Data_Plane [Data Plane - eBPF in Kernel] UP[TLS Uprobes] HX[H Extract] XOR[XOR Path] DNSR[DNS Rewrite - pod netns] CG[Connect Redirect - cgroup hooks] TP[Connect/Close Tracepoints] PROC[Process Tracepoints] TCP[tcp_sendmsg Kprobe] TC[TC Patch - host-side veth] GHASH[TC GHASH Update] end subgraph App [Application] P[Pod with Shadow Secret] end C -->|Creates shadow secrets and syncs BPF maps| UP C -->|Attaches probes to container processes| UP W -->|Rewrites secret references to shadow secrets| P P -->|TLS write with kl:: placeholder| UP UP -->|Tail call: libcrypto-hook processes| HX UP -->|Tail call| XOR HX -->|Tail call| XOR XOR -->|Stores xor_pending| TCP TCP -->|Stores tc_pending| TC TC -->|Tail call| GHASH GHASH -->|Patched ciphertext + tag| Internet DNSR -->|Virtual IPs in DNS answers| P P -->|Connects to a virtual IP| CG CG -->|Redirects to a real address, records the host of the socket| TCP TP -->|Populates conn_ip_map| UP PROC -->|Tracks process lifecycle| C ``` ### Components | Component | Description | |-----------|-------------| | **Controller** (DaemonSet) | Watches Secrets labeled `getkloak.io/enabled=true`, creates shadow secrets with random `kl::…` placeholders of the same length as each real value, syncs real values into eBPF maps, and attaches TLS uprobes to container processes via cgroup discovery. | | **Webhook** (Deployment) | Mutating admission webhook that intercepts Pod creation. Rewrites Secret volume mounts and environment variable references (`secretKeyRef`, `envFrom`) to point to shadow secrets. Evaluates enablement through pod labels or namespace labels. Rejects pods if the shadow secret has not been created yet (fail-closed). Two webhook entries ensure only kloak-enabled namespaces and pods are affected; non-kloak workloads are never impacted, even when the webhook is down. | | **TLS Uprobes** | Attach to `SSL_write` / `SSL_write_ex` (OpenSSL/BoringSSL), `crypto/tls.(*Conn).Write` (Go native), and `SSL_write` at a pre-computed file offset in symbol-stripped Bun binaries. Intercept outbound TLS writes and scan the plaintext for `kl::` placeholders. The plaintext buffer is only read, never modified. | | **H Extract** | Recovers the connection's AES-GCM GHASH key `H`, which is needed to fix the authentication tag after patching. For processes whose `libcrypto` exposes `EVP_CipherInit_ex`, a uprobe captures it at cipher init. Otherwise the `tcp_sendmsg` kprobe walks the library's TLS structs to it. BoringSSL keeps only the AES key schedule, so `H = AES_K(0)` is recomputed in-kernel. | | **XOR Path + TC Patch** | Used for every runtime. Computes `shadow XOR real` for each matched placeholder the pod may use. The `tcp_sendmsg` kprobe keeps only the patches whose host/IP/port policy matches the socket the record leaves on, and bridges them to a tc program on the host side of the pod's veth pair, which XOR-patches the AES-GCM ciphertext in the outgoing packet and recomputes the GHASH tag via a tail call to `tc_ghash_update`. The real secret is never written to user-space memory, and patching outside the pod's network namespace keeps the patched ciphertext out of reach of in-pod packet capture. | | **DNS Rewrite** | A tc program inside the pod's network namespace. For a pod that references a secret restricted to a hostname, it replaces that host's A and AAAA records in answers from a trusted resolver with the host's virtual IPs, and records the real addresses. Other pods get the real answers. The controller attaches it while the container runtime creates the pod's sandbox (NRI), before its containers start. | | **Connect Redirect** | `cgroup/connect4` and `connect6` programs on the pods' cgroups. A connect to a virtual IP goes to one of the host's real addresses, and the socket records the host it is for; `getpeername` still reports the virtual IP. A connect to a virtual IP with no known address is refused. | | **Connect/Close Tracepoints** | Hooks `sys_enter/exit_connect` to track the TCP connections a process makes (fd to destination IP in `conn_ip_map`), which tells them apart from the connections it accepts. Hooks `sys_enter_close` to clean up stale entries. | | **Process Tracepoints** | Hooks `sched_process_exec` and `sched_process_exit` to track container process lifecycle for uprobe attachment and cleanup. | ### Supported Runtimes | Runtime | TLS Library | Hook Point | |---------|------------|------------| | Python, Rust, Ruby, PHP, curl | OpenSSL (libssl.so) | `SSL_write` / `SSL_write_ex` uprobe | | Node.js | OpenSSL (statically linked into `node`) | `SSL_write` uprobe on the main executable | | Apps linked against BoringSSL | BoringSSL (libssl.so) | `SSL_write` uprobe | | Bun (incl. single-executable apps) | BoringSSL (statically linked, symbols stripped) | `SSL_write` uprobe at a per-version file offset (`tools/bun-offsets/`) | | Go | crypto/tls (native) | `crypto/tls.(*Conn).Write` uprobe | Secrets are patched into **AES-128-GCM and AES-256-GCM** records (TLS 1.2 and 1.3). Other ciphers (e.g. ChaCha20-Poly1305) and some libraries (GnuTLS, Go built with `GOEXPERIMENT=boringcrypto`) are not supported yet. ## Host Verification Secrets with `getkloak.io/hosts` annotations are only rewritten on a connection to that host. This prevents secret exfiltration to unauthorized servers, even if an application is compromised. ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant App as Application participant DNS as kube-dns participant RW as eBPF DNS rewrite (pod netns) participant CG as eBPF connect hook participant UP as eBPF uprobe participant KP as eBPF tcp_sendmsg kprobe participant TC as tc patch (host veth) participant Srv as api.stripe.com participant Evil as evil.com Note over App,Evil: 1. DNS Resolution App->>DNS: resolve api.stripe.com DNS-->>RW: A 52.55.108.115 RW-->>App: A 198.18.4.2 (virtual IP of api.stripe.com) Note over App,Evil: 2. TCP Connect App->>CG: connect(198.18.4.2:443) CG->>CG: host of the socket = api.stripe.com CG->>Srv: connect(52.55.108.115:443) Note over App,Evil: 3. TLS Write (Allowed) App->>UP: SSL_write with kl::a1b2c3d4 UP->>UP: stage XOR delta App->>KP: Encrypted record sent on the socket KP->>KP: host of the socket matches allowed_host -> keep the patch KP->>TC: Encrypted record leaves the pod TC->>TC: XOR-patch ciphertext, recompute GCM tag TC->>Srv: Real secret decrypted only by api.stripe.com Note over App,Evil: 4. TLS Write (Blocked) App->>UP: SSL_write to evil.com with kl::a1b2c3d4 UP->>UP: stage XOR delta App->>KP: Encrypted record sent on the socket KP->>KP: socket connected to evil.com, not to a virtual IP -> drop the patch App->>Evil: Placeholder sent as-is ``` ### How Host Verification Works 1. **Virtual IPs** -- The controller gives every hostname in a `getkloak.io/hosts` annotation a stable virtual IP from `controller.ebpf.virtualIPRange` (an IPv4 and an IPv6 range). They are kept in BPF maps pinned on the node, so a controller restart keeps them. 2. **DNS rewrite** -- In the network namespace of each pod that references a secret restricted to the host, a tc program replaces the host's A and AAAA records in answers from a trusted resolver (kube-dns, or `controller.dns.trustedServers`) with its virtual IPs, and records the real addresses. Other pods get the real answers. With NRI (containerd 2.0+, CRI-O 1.30+), the container runtime waits for kloak to set this up before it starts the pod's containers. 3. **Connect redirect** -- A connect to a virtual IP goes to one of the host's real addresses, and the socket records the host it is for. A connect to a virtual IP whose host has no known address fails. The application still sees the virtual IP as its peer. 4. **Secret filtering** -- When the encrypted record is sent, the `tcp_sendmsg` kprobe compares the host of the socket (and the address and port it connected to, for a secret restricted to an IP or a port) with the secret's policy. Match: the patch goes on to the tc program. Mismatch: the patch is dropped and the placeholder is sent as-is, keeping the secret safe. A connection that did not go through a virtual IP (a hardcoded address, DNS over HTTPS) gets no host-restricted secret. 5. **SNI check** -- The socket's host is not enough on its own: CDNs and cloud load balancers serve many customers on the same IPs and route each TLS connection by its SNI, so a compromised app could connect to the virtual IP of `api.stripe.com` while naming another tenant's domain in its ClientHello. A kprobe on `tcp_sendmsg` records the SNI of each connection's first ClientHello, and a secret restricted to a hostname is only rewritten on a connection whose SNI is that host. The comparison is exact and case-insensitive: a client that connects to a short in-cluster name (`my-svc`) does not match an annotation with the full name (`my-svc.ns.svc.cluster.local`), so use the same name in both. Connections without SNI, with an encrypted ClientHello (ECH), or whose ClientHello could not be read are refused. Refusals are logged by the controller as an `SNI check violation`. Set `controller.ebpf.sniCheck: audit` to let them through while logging each one. Secrets restricted to an IP address, or to `*`, are not SNI-checked. ## How It Works ### 1. Label and Annotate Your Secrets Add `getkloak.io/enabled=true` as a label to enable Kloak. Use annotations for host and port filtering. Kloak generates a shadow secret whose values are random `kl::…` placeholders of exactly the same length as the originals. ```yaml apiVersion: v1 kind: Secret metadata: name: api-credentials labels: getkloak.io/enabled: "true" annotations: getkloak.io/hosts: "api.stripe.com" getkloak.io/port: "443" data: api-key: c2stbGl2ZS14eXoxMjM= # sk-live-xyz123 ``` ### 2. Deploy Your Application The webhook automatically rewrites the pod's secret references (volume mounts, `secretKeyRef`, `envFrom`) to use the shadow secret. Your application sees only `kl::…` placeholders and never handles real credentials. ``` # What the application reads from the mounted secret (same length as the real value): kl::q7XmB2rTa9 ``` Only the pods that reference a secret this way can use it. The controller binds each pod's containers to the secrets in its spec, and the data plane refuses to rewrite a placeholder for any other pod: the placeholder goes out unchanged and the controller logs a `secret binding violation`. Apps that read a shadow secret through the Kubernetes API instead of mounting it are refused too. Set `controller.ebpf.secretBinding: audit` to let such rewrites through while logging each one, to find these workloads before enforcing. ### 3. Automatic In-Kernel Rewrite When the application makes an outbound HTTPS request, the eBPF uprobe reads the TLS write and stages a patch, which is kept only if the connection is to an allowed destination (see [Host Verification](#host-verification)). After the TLS library encrypts the record, a tc program on the host side of the pod's veth XOR-patches the ciphertext so that it decrypts to the real secret, and recomputes the AES-GCM tag. The real value never exists in the pod's memory. ``` # What the application writes (and what is in its memory): Authorization: Bearer kl::q7XmB2rTa9 # What api.stripe.com decrypts (after the in-kernel ciphertext patch): Authorization: Bearer sk-live-xyz123 ``` ## Development ```bash make build # Build the kloak binary make test # Run all tests make docker-build # Build Docker image ``` eBPF development requires Linux. On macOS, Kloak uses Lima VMs: ```bash make lima-start # Start Lima VM make generate-ebpf # Generate eBPF Go bindings make test-linux # Run tests in Linux VM make lima-shell # Shell into VM ``` ## License AGPL-3.0
